title: Acute appendicitis: from blocked lumen to the right decision
subject: surgery
summary: Work out why appendicitis hurts where it does, read the signs, choose the right test for each patient and decide who needs the knife, antibiotics or a drain.

objectives.text: Name acute appendicitis as the commonest abdominal surgical emergency, including in pregnancy
Choose the usual obstructing cause for a child versus an adult
Order the events from luminal obstruction to pain shifting to the right iliac fossa, and say why the end artery matters
Pick the true order of symptoms (pain, then vomiting, then fever) and spot a story that does not fit
Tell psoas, obturator and Rovsing signs apart and tie each to the appendix position it suggests
Use the Alvarado score: which items score 2, and what the cut-offs mean
Choose the first imaging test for an adult, a child and a pregnant woman
Pick the step that comes before imaging or surgery in a woman, and the look-alike diagnoses for RIF pain by group
Choose between appendicectomy and antibiotics-first for a given patient
Choose the management of an appendicular mass versus an abscess, and when interval surgery applies
Separate complications of the disease from complications of appendicectomy, and name the nerve at risk with a gridiron incision
Name the commonest appendix tumour and the size rule the PYQ key uses

K1.text: Acute appendicitis is the **most common surgical cause of acute abdomen** (most common abdominal surgical emergency).

K2.text: **Luminal obstruction** is the initiating event: **lymphoid hyperplasia** is the commonest cause in children and young people, a **faecolith (appendicolith)** in adults.

K3.text: The commonest position of the appendix is **retrocaecal**; the second commonest is **pelvic**.

K4.text: The **appendicular artery** (branch of the **ileocolic artery**) is an **end artery**, so thrombosis causes gangrene and perforation.

K5.text: Pain begins **periumbilical** (visceral, T10) and **shifts to the right iliac fossa** when the parietal peritoneum is involved.

K6.text: **Murphy's triad / sequence**: pain first, then vomiting, then fever; vomiting before pain argues against appendicitis.

K7.text: **Alvarado (MANTRELS) score** is out of **10**; tenderness in RIF and leucocytosis score **2** each, every other item scores 1.

K8.text: **Ultrasound** is the first imaging test in children and pregnant women; **contrast-enhanced CT** is the most accurate test in adults.

K9.text: Treatment of choice for acute appendicitis is **appendicectomy**, now usually **laparoscopic**.

K10.text: **Appendicular mass** is treated conservatively by the **Ochsner–Sherren regimen**; an **appendicular abscess** is drained (usually percutaneously, image-guided).

K11.text: Acute appendicitis is acute inflammation of the vermiform appendix.

K12.text: It is classified as **uncomplicated** (inflamed, no gangrene or perforation) or **complicated** (gangrene, perforation, abscess, mass or peritonitis).

K14.text: **Lymphoid hyperplasia** (often after viral infection) predominates in children and adolescents.

K15.text: **Faecolith / appendicolith** predominates in adults; its presence is associated with a higher risk of perforation.

K16.text: Less common causes: foreign bodies, worms (e.g. *Enterobius vermicularis*, *Ascaris*), strictures, and tumours such as **carcinoid** or caecal carcinoma.

K17.text: Peak incidence is in the **second and third decades**.

K21.text: Positions, commonest first: **retrocaecal**, then **pelvic**; subcaecal, pre-ileal and post-ileal positions are less common.

K22.text: The **appendicular artery**, a branch of the **ileocolic artery**, runs in the **mesoappendix** and is an **end artery**.

K23.text: The appendix is rich in **lymphoid tissue**, which is maximal in young people and atrophies with age.

K24.text: Obstruction → continued mucus secretion → rising intraluminal pressure → venous congestion and bacterial overgrowth → mucosal ulceration → transmural inflammation.

K25.text: Rising pressure then compromises arterial supply; because the appendicular artery is an end artery, **gangrene** follows, usually first at the **antimesenteric border**, and then **perforation**.

K26.text: Early distension stimulates **visceral afferents entering at T10**, so pain is referred to the **periumbilical** region.

K27.text: When inflammation reaches the **parietal peritoneum**, pain becomes **somatic and localised to the right iliac fossa**.

K28.text: The **greater omentum** and loops of bowel may wall off the inflamed appendix, forming an **appendicular mass**; pus within it forms an **appendicular abscess**.

K31.text: **Anorexia** is almost constant; nausea and a few episodes of vomiting follow the onset of pain.

K32.text: **Low-grade fever** is usual; a high fever suggests perforation or another diagnosis.

K33.text: **Retrocaecal** appendicitis may give flank or loin pain with little anterior tenderness and little guarding.

K34.text: **Pelvic** appendicitis may cause **diarrhoea**, urinary **frequency** or dysuria (irritation of rectum or bladder), with suprapubic pain.

K37.text: **Rovsing's sign**: pressure in the **left iliac fossa** causes pain in the **right iliac fossa**.

K38.text: **Psoas sign**: pain on **extension of the right hip**; suggests a **retrocaecal** appendix lying on the psoas.

K39.text: **Obturator sign**: pain on **internal rotation of the flexed right hip**; suggests a **pelvic** appendix in contact with obturator internus.

K42.text: **Tenderness on rectal examination** on the right side suggests a **pelvic** appendix.

K47.text: A score of **7 or more** makes appendicitis likely; a low score (≤ 4) makes it unlikely.

K50.text: Diagnosis is primarily **clinical**, supported by scores and imaging.

K53.text: **Urine / serum β-hCG** in every woman of reproductive age to exclude **ectopic pregnancy**.

K54.text: **Ultrasound** (graded compression): **non-compressible, blind-ending tubular structure > 6 mm** in diameter; first-line in **children** and **pregnancy**.

K55.text: **Contrast-enhanced CT** abdomen has the highest sensitivity and specificity in adults and shows complications (abscess, perforation, appendicolith).

K56.text: **MRI** (without gadolinium) is used in pregnancy when ultrasound is inconclusive.

K58.text: Children: **mesenteric lymphadenitis**, gastroenteritis, **Meckel's diverticulitis**, intussusception, right lower lobe pneumonia.

K59.text: Women: **ectopic pregnancy**, ruptured or twisted ovarian cyst, **pelvic inflammatory disease**, mittelschmerz (ruptured Graafian follicle).

K60.text: Adults: ureteric colic, pyelonephritis, perforated peptic ulcer, Crohn's disease (terminal ileitis), caecal diverticulitis.

K61.text: Elderly: **caecal carcinoma**, sigmoid diverticulitis, mesenteric ischaemia.

K63.text: Treatment of choice: **appendicectomy**; **laparoscopic appendicectomy** is preferred where available (less wound infection, less pain, faster recovery, and allows diagnostic laparoscopy, useful in women of reproductive age and the obese).

K65.text: **Gridiron (McBurney's) incision**: oblique, through McBurney's point, perpendicular to the spinoumbilical line; muscles are split along their fibres.

K71.text: **Antibiotics-first (non-operative) treatment** is an accepted option for selected adults with **CT-proven uncomplicated** appendicitis; a significant proportion later need appendicectomy for recurrence, and an **appendicolith** predicts failure.

K73.text: An appendicular mass (lump in RIF usually after 3–5 days of symptoms) is managed conservatively by the **Ochsner–Sherren regimen**: nil by mouth/liquids, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, analgesia, and charting of pulse, temperature and the size of the mass.

K74.text: The regimen is stopped and surgery done if there is rising pulse, increasing pain or mass size, spreading peritonitis or vomiting.

K75.text: **Interval appendicectomy** was traditionally done after **6–8 weeks**; it is now selective, but **colonoscopy or CT is advised in older patients (over about 40)** to exclude **caecal carcinoma**.

K76.text: Treated by **image-guided percutaneous drainage** with antibiotics; open drainage if this fails or is not available.

K79.text: **Appendicular mass** and **appendicular abscess** (including **pelvic abscess** and subphrenic abscess).

K80.text: **Pylephlebitis (portal pyaemia)**: septic thrombophlebitis of the portal venous system, with rigors, jaundice and **liver abscesses**.

K82.text: **Wound infection** is the most common complication after appendicectomy.

K84.text: **Faecal fistula** (from slipped stump ligature, caecal necrosis, or an unrecognised underlying cause such as Crohn's disease, carcinoma or tuberculosis).

K85.text: **Right inguinal hernia** from injury to the **ilioinguinal nerve** with a gridiron incision.

K86.text: **Stump appendicitis** from leaving a long stump.

K89.text: **Carcinoid (neuroendocrine tumour)** is the commonest tumour of the appendix, usually at the **tip**; tumours **< 2 cm** are usually cured by appendicectomy, while larger ones or base involvement need **right hemicolectomy**.

K90.text: **Mucocele** of the appendix may rupture and cause **pseudomyxoma peritonei**.

K91.text: Most common surgical emergency of the abdomen — Acute appendicitis

K92.text: Most common position of appendix — Retrocaecal

K94.text: Most common cause of obstruction (children) — Lymphoid hyperplasia

K95.text: Most common cause of obstruction (adults) — Faecolith / appendicolith

K97.text: Most common non-obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy — Acute appendicitis

K98.text: Initial imaging in children / pregnancy — Ultrasound (graded compression)

K99.text: Investigation of choice in adults (most accurate) — Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen

K100.text: Imaging in pregnancy when USG inconclusive — MRI

K105.text: Most common tumour of appendix — Carcinoid (neuroendocrine tumour)

K106.text: **Rovsing vs psoas vs obturator** is a favourite trap: Rovsing = LIF pressure, RIF pain; psoas = hip extension, retrocaecal; obturator = internal rotation of flexed hip, pelvic.

K107.text: **Alvarado weighting**: only **tenderness in RIF** and **leucocytosis** score 2; the trap option makes migration or rebound score 2.

K108.text: PYQs have expected **ultrasound** as the investigation of choice for appendicitis in general; current practice uses ultrasound first in children and pregnancy and **CECT** as the most accurate test in adults.

K109.text: PYQs have expected **interval appendicectomy at 6–8 weeks** after an appendicular mass; current practice makes routine interval appendicectomy selective, with colonoscopy/CT in older patients to exclude malignancy.

K110.text: PYQs have expected **appendicectomy is the only treatment**; current practice accepts **antibiotics-first** for selected CT-confirmed uncomplicated appendicitis in adults.

K111.text: PYQs have expected **carcinoid > 2 cm → right hemicolectomy**, and **< 2 cm at the tip → appendicectomy alone**.

cards.q: Who is a candidate for antibiotics-first in appendicitis?
cards.a: A selected adult with CT-proven uncomplicated disease and no appendicolith.
Conservative, by the Ochsner-Sherren regimen; stop and operate if pulse, pain or mass size rises or peritonitis spreads.

cards.q: Interval appendicectomy after a mass: old key and current view?
cards.a: Old key 6-8 weeks routinely; now selective, with colonoscopy or CT in patients over about 40.

cards.q: Best treatment for an appendicular abscess?
cards.a: Image-guided percutaneous drainage with antibiotics; open drainage if that fails.

cards.q: Most common complication after appendicectomy, and the nerve at risk with a gridiron incision?
cards.a: Wound infection; ilioinguinal nerve, giving a right inguinal hernia.

cards.q: Order of events from obstruction to gangrene?
cards.a: Obstruction, rising pressure, venous congestion, arterial compromise, then gangrene and perforation.
Tenderness in the right iliac fossa and leucocytosis; every other item scores 1.

cards.a: Psoas: hip extension, retrocaecal. Obturator: internal rotation of flexed hip, pelvic. Rovsing: left fossa pressure, right fossa pain.

cards.q: First imaging in adult, child and pregnancy?
cards.a: Adult: contrast CT, the most accurate. Child and pregnancy: graded-compression ultrasound, then MRI without gadolinium in pregnancy if inconclusive.

cards.q: First step in a woman of reproductive age with RIF pain?
cards.a: Serum or urine beta-hCG, before imaging or surgery.

cards.q: Commonest appendix tumour and the PYQ size rule?
cards.a: Carcinoid, usually at the tip; under 2 cm appendicectomy, over 2 cm right hemicolectomy.

fell_recovered.text: You first put vomiting ahead of pain, then corrected. In appendicitis pain comes first; vomiting first points to gastroenteritis. Keep pain-first as a quick filter when a story seems off.

fell_open.text: You stored the symptoms as an unordered list, so vomiting felt like an opening symptom. In appendicitis pain comes first, then vomiting, then fever; vomiting before pain argues against it. Review the order card and use pain-first to screen vignettes for gastroenteritis.

fell_recovered.text: You misplaced the 2-point items or the meaning of the cut-off, then rebuilt them. Only RIF tenderness and leucocytosis score 2, out of 10; 7 or more is likely, not proof. Re-add from the table when numbers appear in an exam.

avoided.text: You know ultrasound is first-line, not final, in adults. Good.

fell_recovered.text: You first took a negative ultrasound as the end of the work-up, then corrected. In an adult, an unhelpful scan leads on to contrast CT, which is more accurate. Keep that next-step reflex.

fell_open.text: You treated the first-line test as the final word, so a negative or inconclusive ultrasound ended your work-up. In adults, contrast-enhanced CT is the most accurate test and follows an unhelpful scan. Add CECT to your adult imaging ladder and revisit the imaging card.

avoided.text: You read the patient before choosing the test. Children and pregnancy change the first scan.

fell_recovered.text: You first gave CT to a child or pregnant patient, then corrected. Ultrasound comes first in both; CT is the adult answer. When a stem names age or pregnancy, circle it before choosing.

fell_open.text: You applied the adult CT answer to every patient and dropped the age and pregnancy qualifier. Ultrasound is first in children and pregnant women; contrast CT is the most accurate test in adults. Ask 'who is the patient?' first and review the three-group imaging contrast card.

avoided.text: Your pregnancy ladder runs ultrasound, then MRI. Right order.

fell_recovered.text: You first put MRI at the top of the pregnancy ladder, then corrected. Ultrasound is the first rung; MRI without gadolinium is used when ultrasound is inconclusive. Remember accuracy is not the only criterion for a first test.

fell_open.text: You ranked tests by accuracy alone and put MRI first in pregnancy. The first rung is the cheap, safe, available test, graded-compression ultrasound; MRI without gadolinium is the second rung. Redo the pregnancy pathway ordering and keep 'USG, then MRI' as one phrase.

avoided.text: You answer 'investigation of choice' by reading the qualifier. Good exam habit.

fell_recovered.text: You first answered from the older ultrasound key, then corrected. Older keys favoured ultrasound; current practice is ultrasound first in children and pregnancy, CECT most accurate in adults. Keep both as a pair.

fell_open.text: You treated a remembered past-paper key as the current standard and defaulted to ultrasound for adults. Older keys expected ultrasound; current practice uses CECT as the most accurate test in adults. Learn the pair 'USG first, CECT most accurate' and revisit the exam-traps card on it.

avoided.text: Beta-hCG comes first in your plan for women of reproductive age.

fell_recovered.text: You first skipped or delayed the pregnancy test, then corrected. Ectopic pregnancy changes both imaging and surgery, so test first. Under pressure, the favoured diagnosis can crowd this step out.

fell_open.text: You followed the working diagnosis and treated the pregnancy test as an afterthought. In any woman of reproductive age, beta-hCG comes before imaging or theatre, because ectopic pregnancy changes the plan. Re-do the women's step-order card and say 'test pregnancy first'.

avoided.text: You read 'most common' as frequency, not severity.

fell_recovered.text: You first picked a more dramatic emergency, then corrected. Appendicitis is the commonest abdominal surgical emergency, including non-obstetric in pregnancy. Read the qualifier word before the options.

fell_open.text: You read 'most common' as 'most dangerous' or 'most tested' and picked another emergency. Perforated ulcer or cholecystitis may be graver, but appendicitis is the commonest abdominal surgical emergency, in pregnancy too. Underline the qualifier word and review the opening card.

avoided.text: You build a differential by age and sex rather than defaulting to appendicitis.

fell_recovered.text: You first called a look-alike appendicitis, then corrected. Mittelschmerz fits young women with brief mid-cycle pain; caecal carcinoma fits an older man with a mass and anaemia. Keep generating look-alikes for each group.

fell_open.text: You treated the classic pattern as the only pattern, so RIF pain meant appendicitis. Each group has its mimics: mesenteric lymphadenitis in children, mittelschmerz and PID in women, caecal carcinoma in the elderly. Make a three-look-alikes list per group and revisit the differential card.

avoided.text: You check the age before naming the cause of obstruction.

fell_recovered.text: You first gave the cause for the wrong age group, then corrected. Lymphoid hyperplasia predominates in children and young people; a faecolith in adults. Tie it to lymphoid tissue that atrophies with age.

fell_open.text: You ignored the age in the stem and picked the more familiar cause. Lymphoid hyperplasia is commonest in children, faecolith in adults, because lymphoid tissue is maximal when young and atrophies later. Revisit the child-versus-adult contrast card and read the age first.

avoided.text: You keep disease complications and operation complications apart.

fell_recovered.text: You first merged the two complication lists, then rebuilt them. Disease: perforation, mass, abscess, pylephlebitis. Operation: wound infection (commonest), faecal fistula, stump appendicitis. Ask 'disease or knife?' for each item.

fell_open.text: You merged the two complication lists from the same chapter and never asked whether each arises from the disease or the operation. Pylephlebitis, mass and abscess are disease; wound infection, faecal fistula and stump appendicitis follow surgery. Rebuild both lists on paper and redo the which-is-not card.

avoided.text: The gridiron incision and the ilioinguinal nerve are paired in your memory.

fell_recovered.text: You first named a neighbouring nerve, then corrected. The ilioinguinal nerve is injured by a gridiron incision, leading to right inguinal hernia. Draw it on the site if it wobbles.

fell_open.text: You learned the iliac-region nerves as a bundle and picked a neighbour of the nerve at risk. The gridiron incision endangers the ilioinguinal nerve, causing a right inguinal hernia. Sketch the three neighbouring nerves across the gridiron site and review the nerve card.

avoided.text: You separate the exam key from practice: appendicectomy is the treatment of choice, with antibiotics-first for selected patients.

fell_recovered.text: You first held that surgery is the only option, then corrected. Appendicectomy is the treatment of choice; antibiotics-first is accepted for selected uncomplicated cases. Give both in an exam answer.

fell_open.text: You took 'treatment of choice' as 'only treatment', an absolute older keys used. Appendicectomy remains the treatment of choice, but current practice accepts antibiotics-first for selected CT-confirmed uncomplicated adults. Add that to your notes and revisit the treatment contrast card.

avoided.text: You check the qualifiers before offering antibiotics-first.

fell_recovered.text: You first offered antibiotics-first too widely, then corrected. It suits CT-proven uncomplicated disease without an appendicolith; an appendicolith predicts failure. Keep the three conditions together.

fell_open.text: You kept 'antibiotics-first is acceptable' and dropped its conditions. It applies to selected adults with CT-proven uncomplicated disease; an appendicolith or complicated disease points to surgery. Review the three qualifiers on the management card, then redo the patient-comparison question.

avoided.text: You give the old key and the modern view of interval surgery.

fell_recovered.text: You first applied interval surgery to everyone, then corrected. Traditionally it was done at 6-8 weeks; now it is selective, with colonoscopy or CT in older patients to exclude caecal carcinoma. Under pressure, remember the older-patient work-up.

fell_open.text: You treated the old key as fixed policy and applied interval appendicectomy routinely, skipping the malignancy check. Now it is selective, and patients over about 40 need colonoscopy or CT for caecal carcinoma. Revisit the interval-surgery card and add the older-patient work-up.

avoided.text: You pick the right first step for mass and for abscess.

fell_recovered.text: You first chose surgery up front, then corrected. A mass gets the Ochsner-Sherren regimen; a drainable abscess gets image-guided percutaneous drainage with antibiotics. Know when the regimen stops.

fell_open.text: You read 'appendicitis means operate now' and skipped the first step. A stable mass is managed conservatively by the Ochsner-Sherren regimen, stopped if the pulse, pain or mass worsens; an abscess is drained percutaneously. Re-learn the step order on the management card.

E1.text: You tend to swap names between look-alike items that share a category. Next time, anchor each name to its defining movement or feature and say it before choosing.

E2.text: You tend to merge two lists that live in the same chapter. Before picking, ask which list the item belongs to, and rebuild each list from its logic.

E3.text: You tend to run a sequence or direction backwards, starting from the end picture. Narrate the process cause first, 'press here, hurts there' or 'blockage, then pressure'.

E4.text: You tend to read a qualifier or a pattern too narrowly: 'most common' as 'most serious', or a classic picture as the only one. Underline the qualifier, then ask what else fits.

E5.text: You tend to answer from a remembered past-paper key without checking current practice. In such stems, give the old key and the modern view as a pair.

E6.text: You tend to remember numbers by how important they feel rather than by the table. Rebuild scores from their items and re-add them before choosing.

E7.text: You tend to drop the qualifier, such as age, pregnancy or appendicolith, and apply a general answer. Circle the patient detail before looking at the options.

E8.text: You tend to treat the first or most accurate test as the whole pathway. Think in rungs: what comes first, what comes after an unhelpful result.

E9.text: You tend to start with the favoured diagnosis and skip the step that comes first. Ask 'what first, and why' before committing to a plan.

underconfident.text: You tapped Guessing on three or more answers you got right. Your knowledge is ahead of your confidence. Next time, give a one-line reason before answering, and tap Sure when you can.
